intro.title: Totals beside every row
intro.bodyMarkdown:
This section's database is a pub quiz league: `players` in teams, and `games`, one row for each player on each quiz night with their `points`. Open **Tables** to see them.

`SUM(points)` adds up all the rows into one row. Add `OVER ()` and it becomes a **window function**: it still adds up all the rows, but every row stays, with the total beside it:

```
SELECT id, player_id, points,
       SUM(points) OVER () AS total
FROM games
ORDER BY id;
```

The rows a window function looks at are its **window**. Empty brackets mean the window is the whole result. Any aggregate works this way: `COUNT(*) OVER ()`, `AVG(points) OVER ()`, `MAX(points) OVER ()`. Having the total on each row makes comparisons easy, such as each game's share of all the points: `100.0 * points / SUM(points) OVER ()`.

Window functions are worked out after `WHERE`, `GROUP BY` and `HAVING`, just before `ORDER BY`. So the window only sees the rows that are left, and with `GROUP BY` it works over the groups: `SUM(SUM(points)) OVER ()` adds up the group totals.

That order also means `WHERE` can't use a window function: **misuse of window function** is the error. Work the window out in a subquery, then filter outside it:

```
SELECT id, points
FROM (SELECT id, points, AVG(points) OVER () AS average FROM games) AS g
WHERE points > average
ORDER BY id;
```

intro.title: Windows per group: PARTITION BY
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`PARTITION BY` splits the rows into groups, and the window function works within each group. It is like `GROUP BY`, except that the rows stay: each one gets its own group's result beside it.

```
SELECT id, played_on, player_id, points,
       SUM(points) OVER (PARTITION BY played_on) AS night_total
FROM games
ORDER BY played_on, player_id;
```

Every game on the same night gets the same `night_total`. Partition by player instead, and each game shows that player's figure: `AVG(points) OVER (PARTITION BY player_id)` is their season average, next to every game they played.

That puts a row and its group side by side, which is exactly what comparisons need: points minus the night's average, a share of the team's total, whether a game was the player's best.

```
SELECT id, player_id, points,
       MAX(points) OVER (PARTITION BY player_id) AS best,
       points = MAX(points) OVER (PARTITION BY player_id) AS is_best
FROM games
ORDER BY player_id, id;
```

You can partition by several columns, or by a column from a joined table, such as the team: `OVER (PARTITION BY p.team, g.played_on)`.

intro.title: Numbering rows: ROW_NUMBER
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Some window functions only make sense in order. `ROW_NUMBER()` numbers the rows 1, 2, 3, … in the order given by `ORDER BY` inside the `OVER`:

```
SELECT id, played_on, player_id,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY played_on, id) AS n
FROM games
ORDER BY n;
```

The `ORDER BY` inside `OVER` only decides the numbering. The order of the result is still decided by the query's own `ORDER BY` at the end, so you usually write both.

With `PARTITION BY`, numbering starts again at 1 in each group. This numbers each player's games in date order, so their first game is 1:

```
SELECT player_id, played_on,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY player_id ORDER BY played_on) AS game_no
FROM games
ORDER BY player_id, game_no;
```

`ROW_NUMBER` always gives different numbers, even to rows that tie in the `ORDER BY`. Which of two tied rows gets the lower number is then up to the database, and may change. So make the order unique: add a tie-breaker such as the id, or use `RANK` (next lesson) when ties should share a number.

To keep only some numbers, such as each player's first game, number the rows in a subquery and filter outside it.

intro.title: Rankings: RANK and DENSE_RANK
intro.bodyMarkdown:
In a quiz, two players on the same score share a place. `RANK()` does that: rows that tie in the `ORDER BY` get the same rank, and the next rank skips ahead, like 1, 2, 2, 4. `DENSE_RANK()` doesn't skip: 1, 2, 2, 3.

```
SELECT player_id, points,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY points DESC, player_id) AS row_no,
       RANK() OVER (ORDER BY points DESC) AS rank,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY points DESC) AS dense_rank
FROM games
WHERE played_on = (SELECT MIN(played_on) FROM games)
ORDER BY points DESC, player_id;
```

On the first night, Ada and Cora both scored 42: `RANK` puts both first and the next player third, `DENSE_RANK` puts the next player second, and `ROW_NUMBER` still numbers them 1 and 2.

Unlike `ROW_NUMBER`, ranks don't need a tie-breaker to be reliable: tied rows get the same rank whatever order they come in. With `PARTITION BY`, each group is ranked on its own, such as the places on each night.

Ranks work on grouped rows too: rank players by season total with `RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(points) DESC)`.

intro.title: The top rows in each group
intro.bodyMarkdown:
The subqueries section found "the top row in each group" with correlated subqueries. Window functions make it shorter and easier to read: number or rank the rows within each group, then keep the first few.

```
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT player_id, played_on, points,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY player_id ORDER BY points DESC, played_on) AS n
  FROM games
)
SELECT player_id, played_on, points
FROM ranked
WHERE n = 1
ORDER BY player_id;
```

That is each player's best game, with ties going to the earlier night. Change `n = 1` to `n <= 3` for each player's top three.

Choose the function by what should happen with ties. `ROW_NUMBER` keeps exactly as many rows as you ask for, so it needs a tie-breaker that decides which tied row wins. `RANK` keeps every tied row, so `rank <= 3` can return more than three rows. `DENSE_RANK` with `= 2` finds everyone on the second-best score.

intro.title: Running totals
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Put `ORDER BY` inside the `OVER` of an aggregate, and it adds up as it goes: each row gets the total from the start up to that row. That is a **running total**.

```
SELECT player_id, played_on, points,
       SUM(points) OVER (PARTITION BY player_id ORDER BY played_on) AS season_so_far
FROM games
ORDER BY player_id, played_on;
```

Each player's total grows game by game, and starts again for the next player. The other aggregates work the same way: `AVG` gives the average so far, `MAX` the best so far, `COUNT(*)` the games so far.

The rows a running total covers are called its **frame**. With `ORDER BY` and nothing else, the frame runs from the start of the partition to the current row, **and every row that ties with it** in the `ORDER BY`. That catches people out:

```
SELECT id, played_on, points,
       SUM(points) OVER (ORDER BY played_on) AS running
FROM games
ORDER BY id;
```

Every game on the same night shows the same `running` value, the total after the whole night, because those games tie on `played_on`. To add one game at a time, make the order unique: `ORDER BY played_on, id`. (The frames lesson shows how to choose the frame yourself.)

For a running total of groups, total the groups first and run the window over them: `SUM(SUM(points)) OVER (ORDER BY played_on)` after `GROUP BY played_on` gives the league's points so far, night by night.

intro.title: The row before and after: LAG and LEAD
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`LAG(points)` gives the value of `points` from the row before, in the order of the `OVER`'s `ORDER BY`. `LEAD(points)` gives the row after. With `PARTITION BY`, "before" means the player's previous game:

```
SELECT player_id, played_on, points,
       LAG(points) OVER (PARTITION BY player_id ORDER BY played_on) AS previous,
       points - LAG(points) OVER (PARTITION BY player_id ORDER BY played_on) AS change
FROM games
ORDER BY player_id, played_on;
```

A player's first game has no game before it, so `previous` is NULL, and so is `change`. `LEAD` is NULL on the last row of each partition in the same way.

Both take two more arguments: how many rows back or forward (`LAG(points, 2)` is two games ago), and a value to use instead of NULL (`LAG(points, 1, 0)`).

LAG works with any column. With dates, `julianday(played_on) - julianday(LAG(played_on) OVER (…))` is the number of days since the player's previous game.

LAG and LEAD need an order that doesn't tie, or "the row before" isn't well defined. Here each player plays once a night, so `played_on` is enough within a player.

intro.title: Moving windows: frames
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A frame says which rows around the current one an aggregate looks at. You write it after the `ORDER BY` inside `OVER`. This is the average of the player's last three games, the current one and the two before it:

```
SELECT player_id, played_on, points,
       ROUND(AVG(points) OVER (PARTITION BY player_id ORDER BY played_on
                               ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 1) AS last3
FROM games
ORDER BY player_id, played_on;
```

That is a **moving average**. `ROWS BETWEEN start AND end` counts rows. The start and end can be `UNBOUNDED PRECEDING` (the first row of the partition), `n PRECEDING`, `CURRENT ROW`, `n FOLLOWING` and `UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING` (the last row).

A frame can leave out the current row: `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING` is every game before this one, so `MAX(points)` over it is the best score before this game. It is NULL for the first game, because the frame is empty.

`RANGE` frames count by value instead of by rows. With one numeric `ORDER BY`, `RANGE BETWEEN 14 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` takes the rows whose value is up to 14 below the current one. Ordering by `julianday(played_on)` makes that "the last 14 days", however many games that is.

Finally, `EXCLUDE CURRENT ROW` at the end of a frame leaves the current row out, so `AVG(points) OVER (PARTITION BY played_on ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING EXCLUDE CURRENT ROW)` is the average of everyone else that night.

intro.title: Buckets and values: NTILE, FIRST_VALUE and more
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`NTILE(4)` splits the rows, in the `OVER`'s order, into 4 buckets as equal in size as it can, and gives each row its bucket's number: the top quarter is 1. If the rows don't divide evenly, the first buckets get one more row.

```
SELECT id, points,
       NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY points DESC, id) AS quarter
FROM games
ORDER BY quarter, points DESC, id;
```

`FIRST_VALUE(points)` gives the value from the first row of the frame, so with `PARTITION BY player_id ORDER BY played_on` it is the points of the player's first game, on every row. `NTH_VALUE(points, 2)` is the second row's value.

`LAST_VALUE` has a trap. The default frame with `ORDER BY` ends at the current row, so the last row of the frame is the current row itself, and `LAST_VALUE(points)` just gives back `points`. To see the whole partition, give the frame yourself: `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING`.

```
SELECT player_id, played_on, points,
       LAST_VALUE(points) OVER (PARTITION BY player_id ORDER BY played_on
                                ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS last_points
FROM games
ORDER BY player_id, played_on;
```

Two more give positions as fractions. `PERCENT_RANK()` is `(rank - 1) / (rows - 1)`: 0 for the first, 1 for the last. `CUME_DIST()` is the share of rows that come before the current row or tie with it, so the last row gets 1.

intro.title: Named windows, FILTER and streaks
intro.bodyMarkdown:
When several functions use the same window, name it once with a `WINDOW` clause, after `HAVING` and before `ORDER BY`, and write `OVER w`:

```
SELECT player_id, played_on, points,
       LAG(points) OVER w AS previous,
       SUM(points) OVER w AS season_so_far
FROM games
WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY player_id ORDER BY played_on)
ORDER BY player_id, played_on;
```

You can add a frame to a named window where you use it: `OVER (w ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)`. (The named window itself must not have a frame then.)

An aggregate window can also take `FILTER (WHERE …)`, written before `OVER`, so it only counts some rows of its frame: `COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE points >= 40) OVER w` is the number of games of 40 or more so far.

Windows also solve **gaps and islands**: finding runs of things in a row. Number the quiz nights with `DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY played_on)`, and number each player's games with `ROW_NUMBER()`. While a player attends every night, both go up by one each time, so `night - ROW_NUMBER()` stays the same. After a missed night it jumps. Each value marks one streak:

```
WITH numbered AS (
  SELECT player_id, played_on,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY played_on) AS night
  FROM games
)
SELECT player_id, played_on, night,
       night - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY player_id ORDER BY played_on) AS streak
FROM numbered
ORDER BY player_id, played_on;
```

Group by player and streak to get each streak's first and last night and its length.

challenges.hint: Put the streak labels in a second CTE, then group by player_id and streak.
challenges.solution:
WITH numbered AS (
  SELECT player_id, played_on,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY played_on) AS night
  FROM games
),
labelled AS (
  SELECT player_id, played_on,
         night - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY player_id ORDER BY played_on) AS streak
  FROM numbered
)

FROM labelled
GROUP BY player_id, streak
ORDER BY player_id, started;

challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each player's `name` and their longest attendance streak in nights (`longest`). Sort by longest (highest first), then name.
challenges.hint: Count each streak as before, then take the MAX per player and join players.
challenges.solution:
WITH numbered AS (
  SELECT player_id, played_on,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY played_on) AS night
  FROM games
),
labelled AS (
  SELECT player_id,
         night - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY player_id ORDER BY played_on) AS streak
  FROM numbered
),
streaks AS (
  SELECT player_id, COUNT(*) AS nights
  FROM labelled
  GROUP BY player_id, streak
)
SELECT p.name, MAX(s.nights) AS longest
FROM streaks s
JOIN players p ON p.id = s.player_id
GROUP BY p.id, p.name
ORDER BY longest DESC, p.name;

challenges.hint: Group by player; `COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE g.points >= 40)` counts the forties; `RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(g.points) DESC)` gives the place.
challenges.solution:
SELECT p.name, COUNT(*) AS games, SUM(g.points) AS total,
       ROUND(AVG(g.points), 1) AS average, MAX(g.points) AS best,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE g.points >= 40) AS forties,
       RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(g.points) DESC) AS place
FROM games g
JOIN players p ON p.id = g.player_id
GROUP BY p.id, p.name
ORDER BY place, p.name;

                                 ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 1) AS form
FROM games g
JOIN players p ON p.id = g.player_id
ORDER BY p.name, g.played_on;

challenges.title: Medium: Best night
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each player's best game (on a tie, the earlier one): `name`, `played_on` and `points`. Sort by name.
challenges.hint: ROW_NUMBER per player by points DESC, then date; keep 1.
challenges.solution:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT g.player_id, g.played_on, g.points,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY g.player_id ORDER BY g.points DESC, g.played_on) AS n
  FROM games g
)
SELECT p.name, r.played_on, r.points
FROM ranked r
JOIN players p ON p.id = r.player_id
WHERE r.n = 1
ORDER BY p.name;

challenges.title: Hard: In form now
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show the players whose latest game beat their own season average: `name`, the latest points (`latest`) and the season average (`average`, 1 decimal). Sort by name.
challenges.hint: In a CTE: ROW_NUMBER newest first and `AVG(points) OVER (PARTITION BY player_id)`. Keep `n = 1 AND points > average`.
challenges.solution:
WITH g AS (
  SELECT player_id, points,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY player_id ORDER BY played_on DESC) AS n,
         AVG(points) OVER (PARTITION BY player_id) AS average
  FROM games
)
SELECT p.name, g.points AS latest, ROUND(g.average, 1) AS average
FROM g
JOIN players p ON p.id = g.player_id
WHERE g.n = 1 AND g.points > g.average
ORDER BY p.name;

challenges.title: Hard: Improvers
challenges.promptMarkdown: Compare each player's first two games with their last two: show `name`, the points of the first two (`first_two`) and of the last two (`last_two`), only for players whose last two scored more. Sort by name.
challenges.hint: Number each player's games both ways (oldest first and newest first) in a CTE; then group with `SUM(CASE WHEN first_no <= 2 THEN points END)` and the same for the last two, and keep the improvers with HAVING.
challenges.solution:
WITH numbered AS (
  SELECT player_id, points,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY player_id ORDER BY played_on) AS first_no,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY player_id ORDER BY played_on DESC) AS last_no
  FROM games
)
SELECT p.name,
       SUM(CASE WHEN n.first_no <= 2 THEN n.points END) AS first_two,
       SUM(CASE WHEN n.last_no <= 2 THEN n.points END) AS last_two
FROM numbered n
JOIN players p ON p.id = n.player_id
GROUP BY p.id, p.name
HAVING last_two > first_two
ORDER BY p.name;

intro.title: Hard project: Season review
intro.bodyMarkdown:
The season is over, and the league wants a review: the league's points night by night, each month's top scorer, the most consistent players, comebacks after missed nights, the teams on each night, and a summary card for every player.

Each challenge needs more than one window, or a window and a GROUP BY together.

challenges.title: Medium: Night by night
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each night's number (`night`, 1 for the first), `played_on`, its points (`night_points`), the change from the night before (`change`) and the league's running total (`league_so_far`). Sort by date.
challenges.hint: Group by played_on; ROW_NUMBER, LAG and a running SUM, all ordered by played_on.
challenges.solution:
SELECT ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY played_on) AS night, played_on,
       SUM(points) AS night_points,
       SUM(points) - LAG(SUM(points)) OVER (ORDER BY played_on) AS change,
       SUM(SUM(points)) OVER (ORDER BY played_on) AS league_so_far
FROM games
GROUP BY played_on
ORDER BY played_on;

challenges.title: Hard: Top of the month
challenges.promptMarkdown: For each month (`month`, like `2026-09`), show its top scorer or scorers by points that month: `month`, `name` and `month_points`. Sort by month, then name.
challenges.hint: Group by month and player in a CTE (`strftime('%Y-%m', played_on)`), RANK within each month, keep 1.
challenges.solution:
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', g.played_on) AS month, p.name, SUM(g.points) AS month_points,
         RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY strftime('%Y-%m', g.played_on) ORDER BY SUM(g.points) DESC) AS place
  FROM games g
  JOIN players p ON p.id = g.player_id
  GROUP BY month, p.id, p.name
)
SELECT month, name, month_points
FROM monthly
WHERE place = 1
ORDER BY month, name;

challenges.title: Hard: Most consistent
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each player's `name`, `best` and `worst` scores, the `spread` between them, and `place` (DENSE_RANK by spread, smallest first). Sort by place, then name.
challenges.hint: Group by player; `DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY MAX(g.points) - MIN(g.points))`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT p.name, MAX(g.points) AS best, MIN(g.points) AS worst,
       MAX(g.points) - MIN(g.points) AS spread,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY MAX(g.points) - MIN(g.points)) AS place
FROM games g
JOIN players p ON p.id = g.player_id
GROUP BY p.id, p.name
ORDER BY place, p.name;

challenges.title: Hard: Comebacks
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show the games a player played after missing one or more nights, in which they scored above their own season average: `name`, `played_on`, `points` and `missed` (nights missed just before). Sort by name, then date.
challenges.hint: CTE 1: DENSE_RANK night numbers. CTE 2: `night - LAG(night) OVER (…) - 1 AS missed` and `AVG(points) OVER (PARTITION BY player_id) AS average`. Keep `missed > 0 AND points > average`.
challenges.solution:
WITH numbered AS (
  SELECT player_id, played_on, points,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY played_on) AS night
  FROM games
),
checked AS (
  SELECT player_id, played_on, points,
         night - LAG(night) OVER (PARTITION BY player_id ORDER BY played_on) - 1 AS missed,
         AVG(points) OVER (PARTITION BY player_id) AS average
  FROM numbered
)
SELECT p.name, c.played_on, c.points, c.missed
FROM checked c
JOIN players p ON p.id = c.player_id
WHERE c.missed > 0 AND c.points > c.average
ORDER BY p.name, c.played_on;

challenges.title: Hard: Teams each night
challenges.promptMarkdown: For each night and team, show `played_on`, `team`, the team's points (`team_points`), its share of the night's points (`share`, %, 1 decimal) and its `place` that night (RANK). Sort by date, then place, then team.
challenges.hint: Group by night and team; `SUM(SUM(g.points)) OVER (PARTITION BY g.played_on)` is the night total.
challenges.solution:
SELECT g.played_on, p.team, SUM(g.points) AS team_points,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(g.points) / SUM(SUM(g.points)) OVER (PARTITION BY g.played_on), 1) AS share,
       RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY g.played_on ORDER BY SUM(g.points) DESC) AS place
FROM games g
JOIN players p ON p.id = g.player_id
GROUP BY g.played_on, p.team
ORDER BY g.played_on, place, p.team;

challenges.title: Hard: Player cards
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show one card per player: `name`, season `total`, `place` (RANK by total), their `best` score, the date of their best game (`best_on`, the earlier on a tie) and their latest three-game average (`form`, 1 decimal). Sort by place, then name.
challenges.hint: In a CTE, per game: ROW_NUMBER by points DESC then date (`best_no`), ROW_NUMBER newest first (`latest_no`) and the 3-game moving average. Then group by player, picking values with `MAX(CASE WHEN … THEN … END)`, and RANK by `SUM(points)`.
challenges.solution:
WITH g AS (
  SELECT player_id, played_on, points,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY player_id ORDER BY points DESC, played_on) AS best_no,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY player_id ORDER BY played_on DESC) AS latest_no,
         AVG(points) OVER (PARTITION BY player_id ORDER BY played_on
                           ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS last3
  FROM games
)
SELECT p.name, SUM(g.points) AS total,
       RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(g.points) DESC) AS place,
       MAX(g.points) AS best,
       MAX(CASE WHEN g.best_no = 1 THEN g.played_on END) AS best_on,
       ROUND(MAX(CASE WHEN g.latest_no = 1 THEN g.last3 END), 1) AS form
FROM g
JOIN players p ON p.id = g.player_id
GROUP BY p.id, p.name
ORDER BY place, p.name;
